data.title: Week 4
data.subtitle: The Gaining of Independence by Uzbekistan and the Challenges of State-Building

narr: Welcome to Week 4 of our exploration into the History of Uzbekistan. This week, we'll focus on the Soviet period and the path to independence, including nation-building republics, four waves of repression, collectivization, the cotton monoculture, contribution to victory over fascism, resource plundering, perestroika, and the Declaration of Independence.
Let's begin by understanding the key points of this transformative period in Uzbekistan's history.

data.heading: Uzbekistan under Soviet Power
bullets: The USSR created a legal basis for sovereign rights of national republics
Constitution of 1924: voluntary principle of federal structure
Constitution of Uzbek SSR (1927): equal-in-rights and sovereign component
Fayzulla Khodjayev led the government, advancing local interests
Growth of Uzbek representation: 23% to 32.3% (1924-1928)
75% Uzbek representation at lower state levels by 1930

narr: In the early Soviet period, the USSR established a legal framework for Uzbekistan's sovereignty. The 1924 constitution proclaimed the voluntary principle of the federal structure, while the 1927 constitution declared Uzbekistan an equal-in-rights and sovereign component.

Fayzulla Khodjayev led the government, working to advance local interests. During 1924-1928, the share of Uzbeks in central organs grew from 23% to 32.3%, and by the end of 1930, reached 75% at lower levels of state apparatus.

data.heading: Soviet Centralization and Control
bullets: Hyper-centralization intensified from 1920s-1930s
Totalitarian administrative model with ideologized economy
Region existed as raw-material appendage (1920s-1990s)
Replaced centuries-old dynastic statehood with 'nation-building'
Ethnic conflicts sown through new state structures
Characteristics: repression, cult of personality, no private enterprise

narr: However, the USSR methodically intensified hyper-centralization from the 1920s to 1930s, implementing a totalitarian administrative model with an ideologized economy and rigid governance control.

During this period, Uzbekistan existed as a raw-material appendage. The centuries-old dynastic statehood was replaced by 'nation-building' states that sowed ethnic conflicts, with characteristics including repression, the cult of personality, and the absence of private entrepreneurship.

data.heading: Collectivization and Industrialisation
bullets: Curtailment of NEP and return to 'war communism' methods
Establishment of Stalin's dictatorship in mid-1930s
Soviets became decoration of party's monopoly on power
Party and state merged into single apparatus
Institutions of civil society destroyed
Replaced by pseudo-social organisations

narr: The curtailment of the NEP (New Economic Policy) and return to 'war communism' methods created a bureaucratic command system for governing society.

By the mid-1930s, Stalin's dictatorship was firmly established. The soviets became merely decorative as the party maintained a monopoly on power. The party and state merged into a single apparatus, destroying institutions of civil society and replacing them with pseudo-social organisations.

data.heading: Forced Collectivization
bullets: Dehkans forced into kolkhozes under threat of losing land, water, food
Resisters were 'dekulakized' - property confiscated and deported
1930-1933: 40,000 dehkan households 'dekulakized'
31,700 dehkans repressed (deported to 17 special settlements)
By 1933: 5,500+ kulak families deported beyond republic
Over 60,000 further dehkans repressed during 'cleansing'

narr: Collectivization was carried out forcibly, with dehkans (traditional farmers) driven into collective farms (kolkhozes) under the threat of deprivation of land, water and food.

Those who resisted were 'dekulakized' - their property was confiscated and they were deported. From 1930-1933 alone, 40,000 dehkan households were 'dekulakized' and 31,700 dehkans repressed. By 1933, more than 5,500 kulak families had been deported beyond the republic, and during the 'cleansing' of kolkhozes, over 60,000 more dehkans were repressed.

data.heading: Agricultural Impact and Famine
bullets: Ruined agriculture caused famine ending only in 1935
Stalin's formula: sharpening of class struggle on path to socialism
Cotton monoculture: 81.5% of agricultural produce by 1933
93.4% cotton by 1937
Uzbekistan supplied 63% of all-union cotton by 1940
Positive: agricultural output grew 130% by 1940 vs 1924

narr: The ruin of agriculture caused a famine that ended only in 1935. This was justified by Stalin's formula about the sharpening of class struggle on the path to socialism.

The cotton monoculture became dominant - by 1933, cotton accounted for 81.5% of all agricultural produce, rising to 93.4% by 1937. By 1940, Uzbekistan supplied 63% of all-union cotton, freeing the USSR from imports. Despite these changes, gross agricultural output grew by 130% by 1940 compared to 1924.

data.heading: The Four Phases of Soviet Repression in Uzbekistan

cells: National intelligentsia, politicians of alternative development
70% of republican leaders repressed, 41,000 imprisoned, 6,920 shot

narr: Now, let's examine the four phases of Soviet repression in Uzbekistan, which represent critical periods of political oppression.
Phase 1, from the 1920s to early 1930s, involved the rollback from the NEP and targeted the national intelligentsia and politicians advocating alternative forms of development.
Phase 2, from 1936-1939 known as the Great Terror, saw fabricated cases against leadership including Fayzulla Khodjayev and others. By spring 1938, over 70% of republican leaders had been repressed.
Phase 3, from 1946-1953, continued repression against the intelligentsia, financiers, and war participants until Stalin's death.
Phase 4, from 1983-1985, known as the Cotton or Uzbek Affair, was a campaign against corruption that led to the arrest of over 25,000 leaders and economic managers.

data.heading: Phase 1 Repression Details
bullets: Victims accused of nationalism: K. Atabayev, T. Ryskulov, A. Rahimbaev
Cases of Inogamov, 'Group of 18', Kasymov were fabricated
1929: 'Milliy Istiqlol' underground group (85 people) arrested
15 shot, rest sent to camps
'Milliy E'tiqod' members sentenced to death or long terms
Mannan Ramiz, Nasir Saidov, Batu, Hosil Vosilov, Sobir Kadyrov

narr: Let's look deeper at Phase 1 repression. Victims included those accused of nationalism like K. Atabayev, T. Ryskulov, and A. Rahimbaev.

Several cases were fabricated, including those of Inogamov, the 'Group of 18', and Kasymov. At the end of 1929, the underground 'Milliy Istiqlol' group headed by philosopher Munavvar Qari was arrested - 85 people total, with 15 shot and the rest sent to camps.
Members of 'Milliy E'tiqod' including Mannan Ramiz, Nasir Saidov, Batu, Hosil Vosilov, and Sobir Kadyrov were sentenced to death or long prison terms.

data.heading: Phase 2 Repression Details
bullets: Fabricated cases against: Fayzulla Khodjayev, A. Ikramov
S. Segizbayev, A. Karimov, A. Islamov, M. Tursunkhodjayev
All were shot
1937-1939: 'troikas' of NKVD imprisoned 41,000+
6,920 were shot
National intelligentsia destroyed: Abdulla Qodiriy, Abdulhamid Chulpon

narr: During Phase 2, the Great Terror, fabricated cases were made against leadership including Fayzulla Khodjayev (chairman of the Council of People's Commissars) and A. Ikramov (first secretary of the Central Committee).
Others targeted included S. Segizbayev, A. Karimov, A. Islamov, and M. Tursunkhodjayev - all were eventually shot.

From 1937-1939 alone, the 'troikas' of the NKVD imprisoned more than 41,000 people, of whom 6,920 were shot. The national intelligentsia was systematically destroyed, including notable figures like Abdulla Qodiriy and Abdulhamid Chulpon.

data.heading: Literacy and Educational Development
bullets: Literacy grew from ~11% (1928) to 68% (1939)
1940: 5,504 general-education schools
Compulsory primary education introduced
Transition to universal seven-year schooling began
1928: 1,400 engineers/technicians; 1940: 6,000

narr: Despite the repression, there were significant developments in education and literacy. Literacy rates grew from approximately 11% in 1928 to 68% by 1939.

By 1940, there were 5,504 general-education schools with 1,368,800 pupils, compared to just 82,300 in 1924. Compulsory primary education was introduced, and the transition to universal seven-year schooling began.
The number of engineers and technicians in industry also increased dramatically, from 1,400 in 1928 to 6,000 by 1940.

data.heading: Professional Development and Cultural Impact
bullets: By 1941: 55,300 specialists with diplomas
20,200 with higher education
35,100 with secondary specialized education
Negative: Change of writing systems caused new illiteracy
Private schools liquidated
Prison terms for publication in Arabic script

narr: Professional development also progressed significantly. By January 1, 1941, the republic had 55,300 specialists with diplomas - 20,200 with higher education and 35,100 with secondary specialized education.

However, there were significant negative cultural impacts. The change of writing systems led to a new wave of illiteracy, private schools were liquidated, and prison terms of 10-15 years were imposed for publication in the Arabic script.

The Soviet system imposed Soviet rites, promoted accelerated 'internationalization', curtailed the appointment of national cadres, and promoted a culture described as 'socialist in content, internationalist in spirit, national in form,' leading to the alienation of the people from their traditional culture.
